content: 1. Training health facility staff on breastfeeding and supportive feeding practices, compared to not providing such training, aims to increase the rates of early initiation of breastfeeding. This training can be tailored based on the type of staff (e.g., clinical roles, those with limited involvement in infant feeding support, or specialists in infant feeding support) and the frequency of training sessions (e.g., one-time, twice, or at least three times). Outcomes include early initiation of breastfeeding, exclusive breastfeeding during the facility stay, duration of exclusive breastfeeding, healthcare workers' knowledge of infant feeding, staff skills in improving maternal feeding practices, attitudes toward infant feeding, and adherence to the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes. 2. Providing antenatal breastfeeding education to mothers, compared to not offering such education, is intended to increase exclusive breastfeeding rates during the facility stay. This education can be delivered through various methods, such as face-to-face counseling, printed materials, or group sessions, and at different frequencies (e.g., one-time, twice, three times, or at least four times). Outcomes include exclusive breastfeeding during the facility stay, early initiation of breastfeeding within one hour after birth, exclusive breastfeeding at one, three, and six months, the duration of exclusive breastfeeding, and the onset of lactation. 3. Linking mothers giving birth in maternity and newborn care facilities to continuing breastfeeding support after discharge, compared to not providing such linkage, aims to increase exclusive breastfeeding rates at one month. This support may include scheduling follow-up visits, referrals to peer support, sharing information, or providing a contact number. The quality of support can vary based on the training or background of the support provider (e.g., no training or lactation support training). Outcomes include exclusive breastfeeding at one, three, and six months, the duration of exclusive breastfeeding, the duration of any breastfeeding, and infant morbidity (e.g., respiratory infections, diarrhea). 4. Immediate or early skin-to-skin contact between mothers and their healthy newborns, compared to standard contact, has been shown to positively impact the establishment and maintenance of breastfeeding and infant physiology. This conclusion is based on 46 randomized controlled trials involving 3,850 women and their healthy term infants, conducted in countries such as Canada, Chile, China, Germany, and others. 5. Kangaroo mother care (KMC) for low-birth-weight infants, compared to conventional neonatal care, has been evaluated for its potential to reduce morbidity and mortality. This includes early-onset KMC versus late-onset KMC. The review included 21 randomized controlled trials with 3,042 infants from countries such as Australia, Colombia, Ecuador, and others. 6. Delayed initiation of breastfeeding has been associated with increased infant mortality and morbidity. A systematic review and meta-analysis examined this relationship in infants who initiated breastfeeding, based on five studies involving 136,047 infants from countries like Ghana, India, and Tanzania. 7. Showing mothers how to breastfeed and providing additional support for healthy breastfeeding mothers with healthy term babies has been evaluated in 100 trials involving 83,246 mother-infant pairs. These studies were conducted in countries such as Australia, Bangladesh, Belarus, Brazil, and others. 8. The use of feeding-readiness instruments for preterm infants, compared to no instrument or another instrument, has been assessed for its effects on the time to establish full oral feeding and the duration of hospitalization. However, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. 9. Methods of milk expression for lactating women have been evaluated for their acceptability, effectiveness, safety, impact on milk composition, contamination, and costs. This review included 41 trials with 2,293 participants from countries such as Australia, Brazil, Canada, and others. 10. Rooming-in, where mothers and infants stay together, compared to separate care, has been assessed for its impact on the duration of breastfeeding. One trial involving 176 women in Russia was included in the review. 11. Baby-led breastfeeding, compared to scheduled or mixed breastfeeding, has been evaluated for its effects on successful breastfeeding in healthy newborns. However, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. 12. Responsive feeding for preterm infants, compared to scheduled feeding, has been assessed for its impact on growth rates, parent satisfaction, and time to hospital discharge. Nine randomized controlled trials with 593 infants were included, but none reported on critical outcomes. 13. The early introduction of additional foods or fluids for healthy breastfed full-term infants has been evaluated for its benefits and harms. This review included 11 trials with 2,542 randomized mother-infant pairs from countries such as the Czech Republic, Sweden, and the United States. 14. Restricted versus unrestricted pacifier use in healthy full-term newborns, whose mothers intend to exclusively breastfeed, has been assessed for its impact on breastfeeding duration and infant health. Three trials involving 1,915 babies from countries like Argentina, Canada, and Switzerland were included. 15. Non-nutritive sucking for preterm infants has been evaluated for its effects on physiological stability and nutrition. This review included 12 trials with 746 preterm infants from countries such as Australia, Brazil, China, and others. 16. Oral stimulation for promoting oral feeding in preterm infants has been assessed for its effectiveness. However, the details of this review were not fully provided in the text.
